1.pericope_label: A certain man was sick, named Lazarus: this sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God

schools.summary: Barnes and Clarke explain John’s sole record by the danger to a living Lazarus, and date the interval from the dedication; Robertson derives Lazarus from Eleazar and, with Ellicott and Lightfoot, resists merging Mary of Bethany with the sinner of Luke 7 or with Magdalene.
Calvin sets the miracle at the close of Christ’s life as a lively image of our own resurrection, power displayed on a rotting corpse, and rejects the legend that made Bethany a castle.
Clarke declines to fix the chronology beyond the evidence; Wesley reads “not unto death” as denying not death but its permanence.
Henry hears the sisters’ plea resting wholly on Christ’s love and not their own: not he who loveth thee, but he whom thou lovest.
Chrysostom distinguishes this Mary from the harlot of Luke and explains the sending rather than coming by confidence and grief; Theophylact adds that women should not leave the house.

Augustine hears restraint in a message that neither asks a cure nor prescribes one; Bede reads the name Lazarus as “helped”; Augustine of Hippo bids us rejoice rather than wonder, creation being the greater work.

debates.question: Is the anointing that identifies Mary a past act or a forward reference to chapter 12?

positions.view: A former anointing, which explains the family’s confidence in sending
A proleptic reference to the anointing John narrates later

debates.question: How far does “for the glory of God” reach?

positions.view: To the raising of Lazarus and the Son’s glory in it
Forward as well, the illness being the immediate cause of the Son of Man’s own death

outliers.claim: Guards the clause from proving too much: God is glorified in the ruin of the reprobate also, so Christ speaks here only of what belongs to his saving office.
Illustrates the name Martha from the Talmud’s Martha daughter of Boethus, who had tapestry laid to the Temple and was later dragged behind Arabian horses.

themes: Now a certain man was sick, named Lazarus, of Bethany, the town of Mary and her sister Martha.
(It was that Mary which anointed the Lord with ointment, and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was sick.)
Therefore his sisters sent unto him, saying, Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick.
When Jesus heard that, he said, This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God might be glorified thereby.

5.pericope_label: He abode two days still in the same place: are there not twelve hours in the day?

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the Evangelist’s word for love a matter of who is speaking rather than who is loved, refuses the usual explanations of the delay in favour of the appointed hour, and with Barnes reckons the four days from the journey; Robertson reads the imperfect as continued love.

Calvin warns against judging God’s love by the condition before our eyes, since delay increases ardour and exercises patience, and makes the calling of God the daylight in which a man walks safely; Gill separates everlasting love from the particular human affection.

Clarke rules that Christ never denies a lesser favour but to confer a greater, and puts the twelve hours into Christ’s own mouth: I am immortal till my work is done; Wesley reports the Jewish reckoning of the day.
Henry compresses the figure: light in us is to moral actions what light about us is to natural.
Chrysostom and Alcuin explain the delay as allowing death and burial, that none might call it a trance; Theophylact alone reads day and night as the time before the Passion and the Passion itself.
Augustine notes he returned to the place he had just escaped — leaving as man, in weakness, returning in power — and allegorises the twelve hours of the appointed disciples.

debates.question: Why did Christ delay two days?

positions.view: To allow death and burial beyond dispute
Because every hour has its own appointed work, not to test a faith already shown
To exercise the patience of those who prayed

outliers.claim: Reads the disciples’ concern for their Master as a plausible cover for fear of their own danger, as men still dread the cross and hide indolence behind excuses.

themes: Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus.
When he had heard therefore that he was sick, he abode two days still in the same place where he was.
Then after that saith he to his disciples, Let us go into Judea again.
His disciples say unto him, Master, the Jews of late sought to stone thee; and goest thou thither again?
Jesus answered, Are there not twelve hours in the day? If any man walk in the day, he stumbleth not, because he seeth the light of this world.
But if a man walk in the night, he stumbleth, because there is no light in him.

11.pericope_label: Our friend Lazarus sleepeth: Lazarus is dead, and I am glad for your sakes that I was not there

schools.summary: Robertson notes the perfect of the verb behind “cemetery”; Barnes takes sleep as tender by design, holding out a resurrection; Ellicott traces the twin figures of sleep and death to Homer and explains the disciples’ mistake from the rabbinic list of favourable symptoms.

Calvin denies the pious etymology of sleep, since profane writers use it as freely, and acquits the disciples of craft while noting they seized gladly on a reason not to go; he generalises that works near the ordinary course of nature are less valued, so deliverance had to be delayed.

Clarke reports the idiom as common among the Jews and answers the charge of peevishness in Thomas with a rule of charitable construction; Wesley calls sleep the language of heaven for the death of good men.
Henry turns the figure to comfort, death being better than sleep as the end of earthly cares rather than a pause in them.

Chrysostom hears a second consolation in the errand to Bethany, meets the objection that the disciples must have understood, marks the miracle left unannounced, and looks past Thomas’s weakness to the man who later crossed the earth; Theophylact reduces the gladness to a line.
Augustine refuses to treat sleep as euphemism — asleep to the Lord, dead to men who could not raise him; Bede sees in Thomas an appearance of firmness in one unmindful, like Peter, of his frailty.

positions.view: Because raising the dead is as easy to God as waking a sleeper is to us
Because a corpse lies without feeling, as profane writers also use the word
To intimate that death is not final and remove what is dreadful in it

debates.question: With whom did Thomas propose to die?

positions.view: With Christ, whose danger he foresaw
With Lazarus, the words then being ironical

outliers.claim: Lays down a rule of interpretation for another man’s words — where a saying touching character will bear both senses, take the favourable one, though most men feed like flies, passing over the whole man to light on his sores.

themes: These things said he: and after that he saith unto them, Our friend Lazarus sleepeth; but I go, that I may awake him out of sleep.
Then said his disciples, Lord, if he sleep, he shall do well.
Howbeit Jesus spake of his death: but they thought that he had spoken of taking of rest in sleep.
Then said Jesus unto them plainly, Lazarus is dead.
And I am glad for your sakes that I was not there, to the intent ye may believe; nevertheless let us go unto him.
Then said Thomas, which is called Didymus, unto his fellowdisciples, Let us also go, that we may die with him.

17.pericope_label: He had lain in the grave four days already: Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died

schools.summary: Lightfoot measures the Jewish mile and reckons the furlong from the numeral value of its letters, and describes the seven standings and sittings of the mourners; Barnes quotes a traveller on the reputed sepulchre; Ellicott hears in John’s past tense a writer whose Jerusalem no longer stood, and Robertson catches the imperfect that leaves Mary sitting.

Calvin turns the visitors’ kindness into providence — assembled by a secret decree so the miracle should not rest on the household’s testimony — and judges Martha’s confidence to rest on no promise of Christ, so that only a few sparks of faith shine through.

Clarke sets out the thirty days of mourning and concludes the sisters thought Christ could cure at hand but not at a distance, taking him for no more than a prophet; Wesley finds in Martha’s next words a hope she dare not speak.

Henry dates the death to the moment Christ said “our friend sleepeth”, draws from it that promised salvations come surely but slowly, and reads the sisters’ different conduct as the advantage and the snare of their natural tempers.

Chrysostom does the arithmetic of the four days, asks how these Jews could console the friends of one they had resolved to expel, and says Martha went alone to speak with Christ by herself; Theophylact adds her fear that the visitors would follow.

Augustine turns the four days into four deaths — the law of birth, natural law transgressed, written law despised, the Gospel transgressed — and defends Martha’s reticence as leaving the matter to Christ’s judgment; Alcuin says the delay made the raising more glorious.

debates.question: How much faith is in “if thou hadst been here”?

positions.view: A faith that ties saving power to bodily presence, taking Christ for a prophet
Presumption resting on no promise, only sparks of faith
Modesty that leaves the outcome to his judgment

outliers.claim: Reports that the seven standings and sittings on the way back from the grave were ordained, on one account he has seen, because evil spirits followed from the tomb and needed that time to leave.

themes: Then when Jesus came, he found that he had lain in the grave four days already.
Now Bethany was nigh unto Jerusalem, about fifteen furlongs off:
And many of the Jews came to Martha and Mary, to comfort them concerning their brother.
Then Martha, as soon as she heard that Jesus was coming, went and met him: but Mary sat still in the house.
Then said Martha unto Jesus, Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.
But I know, that even now, whatsoever thou wilt ask of God, God will give it thee.

23.pericope_label: I am the resurrection, and the life: believest thou this?

schools.summary: Ellicott reads Martha’s retreat as the most human moment in the chapter, dwells on the emphatic pronoun that makes resurrection a present person rather than a distant date, and guards “never die” as denying not the fact of death but its sting; Robertson takes from Westcott that resurrection is one manifestation of the Life, and ranks Martha’s confession above Peter’s; Barnes and Lightfoot supply the doctrine and the rabbinic foil.

Calvin forgives Martha the fault of fabricating hope and then the opposite fault of stopping short when Christ stretches out his hand, makes faith a spiritual resurrection of the soul against those who think nature prepares men for grace, and grounds perpetual life on Christ’s power to finish what he began.

Clarke reads the promise flatly as immediate, and turns the claim into a question — by whom shall he rise, if not by me, and is it not as easy now as then?; Wesley reduces the saying to the resurrection of the dead and the life of the living.

Chrysostom finds a middle course between asking God and disclaiming help, argues that one needing help could not be the resurrection, and doubts Martha understood, being asked one thing and answering another.
Augustine marks the deliberate ambiguity, that he does not say now; Alcuin gives the logic in a line, that he is the resurrection because he is the life.

debates.question: Does Martha’s confession show understanding or its lack?

positions.view: Heroic faith, outranking Peter’s because made with her brother four days buried
Assent without comprehension — asked one thing, she answers another

outliers.claim: Answers the rabbis on their own ground with the bone luz that water would not steep nor fire burn, which Hadrian was shown as the seed of resurrection, and asks why they never mauled the Sadducees with the argument.

themes: Jesus saith unto her, Thy brother shall rise again.
Martha saith unto him, I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day.
Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live:
And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this?
She saith unto him, Yea, Lord: I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God, which should come into the world.

28.pericope_label: The Master is come, and calleth for thee: Mary fell down at his feet

schools.summary: Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the household title to be Teacher rather than Rabbi, note that Martha reports only what she herself heard, and judge the crowd of consolers to have meant kindly and done the one wrong thing; Lightfoot cites the rule against following a woman on the road and then withdraws it.

Calvin thinks Christ stayed outside the village at Martha’s request, since his escape from stoning was fresh, and turns the mourners’ kindness against them: the bereaved are eager to increase their grief by every method, and friends who indulge that excess do them little good; Gill supplies the topography.

Clarke assumes Christ did ask for Mary, to strengthen her faith beforehand, and reports the custom of visiting the grave during the three days of weeping; Wesley notes that Martha had not fallen at his feet.

Chrysostom explains the secrecy and the slow approach, finds Mary the more fervent for forgetting the crowd, and in his homilies observes that mourning women wish to be made much of on account of their case; Theophylact adds her fear the visitors would follow.

Augustine glosses “secretly” as in a low voice and infers from Mary’s haste that she would not have let Martha go alone had she known; Bede says she could not bring out what she wanted for weeping; Alcuin turns her words into a compliment.

debates.question: Was the crowd’s following Mary a defeat of the plan or a providence?

positions.view: A well-meant blunder that undid Martha’s secrecy
A providence securing witnesses to the miracle

outliers.claim: Reads Mary’s prostration as an implicit confession, since nothing about Christ after the flesh was royal enough to draw such honour, while still charging her with tying an infinite power to a bodily presence.

themes: And when she had so said, she went her way, and called Mary her sister secretly, saying, The Master is come, and calleth for thee.
As soon as she heard that, she arose quickly, and came unto him.
Now Jesus was not yet come into the town, but was in that place where Martha met him.
The Jews then which were with her in the house, and comforted her, when they saw Mary, that she rose up hastily and went out, followed her, saying, She goeth unto the grave to weep there.
Then when Mary was come where Jesus was, and saw him, she fell down at his feet, saying unto him, Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.

33.pericope_label: He groaned in the spirit, and was troubled: Jesus wept

schools.summary: Ellicott distinguishes the calm shedding of tears from the cry of lamentation and turns the verse into an apology — a God in tears has drawn the stoic’s smile, yet humanity has never seen the divinity of the Son of Man more clearly; he also separates the two parties among the bystanders, the second inferring that this failure discredits the healing of the blind man. Robertson reads an ingressive aorist of a verb that never means to wail, and notes they say could not rather than cannot. Barnes concludes that religion neither forbids nor condemns such grief.

Calvin weighs the two parties, finding the first more modest for allowing Christ nothing beyond a man than the second who praise his power to reproach him with withholding it, and diagnoses a twofold disease in men who complain the moment God declines a wish.

Clarke is indignant that certain ancients thought weeping a degradation and struck from Luke the place where Christ wept over Jerusalem, and calls the sceptics’ reasoning madness; Wesley marvels that men who thought he might have prevented death never dreamed he could undo it.
Henry fastens on the idiom “he troubled himself”, concluding he was never troubled but voluntarily, and observes that we never read he laughed but more than once find him in tears.

Theophylact says he gave his nature vent or restrained it as suited the lesson, since absence of sympathy is brutal and excess of it unmanly; Chrysostom says his enemies turned against him the very works that should have proved his power.

Augustine answers that he was troubled because it pleased him, as he hungered because it pleased him, and asks why Christ wept if not to teach men to weep; Alcuin says he wept in the nature by which he could not raise.

positions.view: Condescension to the bystanders, that they might be witnesses
A voluntary self-troubling proper to the higher nature
Instruction in the due measure of grief

outliers.claim: Reports on Epiphanius that ancients improperly styled fathers of the Church excised Christ’s weeping over Jerusalem from Luke as a degradation of his character.

themes: When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews also weeping which came with her, he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled,
And said, Where have ye laid him? They said unto him, Lord, come and see.
Jesus wept.
Then said the Jews, Behold how he loved him!
And some of them said, Could not this man, which opened the eyes of the blind, have caused that even this man should not have died?

38.pericope_label: Take ye away the stone: if thou wouldest believe, thou shouldest see the glory of God

schools.summary: Robertson renders the idiom as “he is a fourth-day man”, an ordinal Herodotus uses of one four days dead, and notes the verb means only to give out an odour; Ellicott alone questions the inference, since the text never says decomposition had begun and the sepulchre stood open while Jesus prayed; Lightfoot supplies the three-day belief about the hovering spirit and the changed face.

Calvin sees a champion preparing for a contest rather than an idle spectator, judges Martha to measure an incomprehensible power by the perception of her flesh, and makes faith the condition under which the glory is displayed, unbelief keeping God’s hands shut; Gill notes the opened grave broke a rabbinic rule.
Clarke asks how, on the vertical arrangement of the tomb, Lazarus could have come forth at all; Wesley says in six words that reason and faith struggled together.
Henry draws the line exactly: men may prepare the way and take away the stone, and Christ alone gives life.

Chrysostom answers why the stone was not moved by a word — that the miracle should happen in full sight and none say, as of the blind man, that this was not the same person; Theophylact hears weakness of faith in Martha’s protest; Cyril of Jerusalem draws out that some are saved by others’ faith, the sisters supplying what the dead man lacked.
Origen draws the rule that nothing should come between Jesus’ commands and the doing of them.
Augustine also hears weakness of faith, while Bede takes her words for wonder rather than despair.

debates.question: Had the body actually begun to decay?

positions.view: Assumed by the expositors generally from the fourth day
Not stated in the text, and told against by the interval when the sepulchre stood open

debates.question: Do Martha’s words express despair or wonder?

positions.view: Weakness of faith
Wonder rather than despair

outliers.claim: Makes the sisters’ faith supply the dead man’s own, so that faith exercised on another’s behalf recalled him from the gates of hell.

themes: Jesus therefore again groaning in himself cometh to the grave. It was a cave, and a stone lay upon it.
Jesus said, Take ye away the stone. Martha, the sister of him that was dead, saith unto him, Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been dead four days.
Jesus saith unto her, Said I not unto thee, that, if thou wouldest believe, thou shouldest see the glory of God?

41.pericope_label: Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me: Lazarus, come forth

schools.summary: Robertson infers a prayer already offered and answered before the act, quoting Dods that there is no pomp of incantation but simple thanksgiving, and notes the command is two adverbs without a verb; Ellicott corrects the tense, presses the emphatic pronoun as the law of Christ’s human life, and refuses to make the bound man’s walking a second miracle, since the order to loose him tells against it; Lightfoot takes the opposite view.

Calvin makes the lifted eyes posture and not rule, since the publican pierced heaven with his face to the ground, and reads the last command as evidential — Christ could have loosed the bands himself but employed the spectators’ hands as witnesses — turning sharply on those who draw auricular confession from the words.
Clarke explains the audible prayer by the current belief that great wonders might be worked by the devil’s power, so that the supreme God was invoked openly.

Chrysostom denies that “thou hast heard me” confesses any lack of power, calling it the language of friends and equals, and marks that Christ says neither arise nor in my Father’s name; Theophylact takes the loud voice for the trumpet of the general resurrection, raised against the fable that the soul stayed in the tomb.
Origen reads the lifted eyes as the lifting of the mind, and makes Christ’s prayer the pattern of our own.

Augustine says the calling by name was necessary lest all the dead come out, and with Gregory reads the loosing as confession and absolution; Hilary states the case exactly, that he prayed not from need but for our instruction; Alcuin divides the labour between Christ who wakes and the ministry that absolves.

debates.question: What does the last command mean?

positions.view: An evidential act, employing the spectators as witnesses, and addressed to the Jews rather than the disciples
A word to the ministers, the loosing of sins figured in the loosing of the bands

debates.question: Was the bound man’s walking itself a miracle?

positions.view: Yes, a wonder within a wonder
No, and the order to loose him tells against it

outliers.claim: He did not need to pray but prayed for our sakes: the prayer benefited not himself but our faith — he wanted no help, we wanted instruction.

themes: Then they took away the stone from the place where the dead was laid. And Jesus lifted up his eyes, and said, Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me.
And I knew that thou hearest me always: but because of the people which stand by I said it, that they may believe that thou hast sent me.
And when he thus had spoken, he cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth.
And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go.

45.pericope_label: Many believed on him; but some went to the Pharisees: what do we? for this man doeth many miracles

schools.summary: Robertson observes that the Sadducean priesthood now takes the lead, supported by its own opponents, and that Lazarus is never named in the debate though plainly included in the many signs; Ellicott hears in the present tense the confession of men who feel they have delayed too long, and marks the contradiction in a sentence granting many signs while calling him only this Man; Barnes supplies the theory that let them grant the works and refuse the claim; Lightfoot believes the council knew whom it condemned.
Calvin says they assemble deliberately to bury a glory that astonishes them, setting their own industry as a shield against divine power as if perseverance could vanquish God.

Clarke observes that Pharisees as such could not convene a council, and that the miracle was so incontestable they were at their wit’s end, their own spies having borne the testimony; Wesley answers their question in four words — what do we? believe.
Henry makes the informers witnesses against themselves, acknowledging his credentials and denying his commission, and holds that perverting what is true is as bad as forging what is false.

Chrysostom asks what evidence there was of an usurper in one who chose desert places, and says they declared the state in danger lest they seem to consult their own interest; Theophylact notes that a miracle which should have drawn wonder became the occasion of a plot.
Origen judges the informers to be of the unbelieving party, since the believers are the larger group, and finds both audacity and blindness in men who own the miracles yet expect to prevail.
Augustine says the wretched men considered only how to kill him, not how to be saved, and that fearing to lose temporal things they lost both.

debates.question: Who were the men who reported to the Pharisees?

positions.view: Unbelievers meaning to inflame the authorities
Possibly believers hoping to conciliate them — a reading Origen states and rejects

debates.question: Was the fear of Rome sincere?

positions.view: A pretext colouring malice, the gospel being no threat to kings or provinces
A real dread of losing temporal things, which cost them both

outliers.claim: Believes the Sanhedrin knew or strongly suspected whom they condemned, since the vinedressers say “this is the heir” and the council knew Daniel’s weeks were accomplished.

themes: Then many of the Jews which came to Mary, and had seen the things which Jesus did, believed on him.
But some of them went their ways to the Pharisees, and told them what things Jesus had done.
Then gathered the chief priests and the Pharisees a council, and said, What do we? for this man doeth many miracles.
If we let him thus alone, all men will believe on him: and the Romans shall come and take away both our place and nation.

49.pericope_label: It is expedient that one man should die for the people: he prophesied that Jesus should die for that nation

schools.summary: Barnes explains the office as originally for life and cautions that prophecy here is not used strictly; Ellicott derives Caiaphas from Cephas and hears in the thrice-repeated phrase a solemnity marking that fatal and decisive year; Robertson allows him the point that no solution had been offered, notes the preposition will bear “instead of”, and remarks drily that politicians are often willing to sacrifice the other fellow; Lightfoot asks bluntly whether Caiaphas is among the prophets.

Calvin denies that the phrase means an annual office, the dignity having become purchasable contrary to a Law that meant it to end only with the holder’s death; he restates the maxim as a resolve to provoke God’s wrath in order to prosper, and gives Caiaphas two tongues, one vomiting his own design while God turned the other to a prediction.

Clarke concedes the maxim is sound politics but answers that we may not do evil that good may come and that none of the premises were certain; he compares Virgil’s line that one life shall fall that many may be saved; Wesley reads the reproof as aimed at slow deliberation.
Henry makes the dying both attraction and centre, gathering those far from Christ and uniting those far from each other.

Chrysostom says divine grace used the high priest’s mouth but never touched his corrupt heart; in his homilies he notes that what the others put forward doubtfully this man cried aloud, shamelessly and audaciously.
Origen separates the act from the character — not everyone who prophesies is a prophet — and denies that the resolve to kill came from the same Spirit as the prophecy.

Augustine reads the Evangelist’s enlargement as a correction, since there were other sheep not of that fold; Gregory observes that killing him to extinguish his followers’ devotion made faith grow from the very thing meant to destroy it.

debates.question: In what sense did Caiaphas prophesy?

positions.view: By the virtue of the office, grace using his mouth without touching his heart
By the year rather than the office, some drops of that outpouring falling on a wicked man
Not in the strict sense of prophecy at all

outliers.claim: Cites Virgil’s Neptune — one life shall fall that many may be saved — as an episode neither historical nor ornamental, introduced purely to state the poet’s creed on vicarious atonement.

themes: And one of them, named Caiaphas, being the high priest that same year, said unto them, Ye know nothing at all,
Nor consider that it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not.
And this spake he not of himself: but being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus should die for that nation;
And not for that nation only, but that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad.
Then from that day forth they took counsel together for to put him to death.

54.pericope_label: He went unto a city called Ephraim: what think ye, that he will not come to the feast?

schools.summary: Ellicott sets out the uncertainty about Ephraim, the manuscripts spelling it four ways and Eusebius and Jerome differing by twelve miles, and points out that the Law ordained no special purification before the passover; Robertson notes the manhunt is now in earnest and finds in a perfect participle the knots of people about the temple precincts; Lightfoot reports the graduated times of purifying; Barnes sets danger against duty.

Calvin declines the topographical search, since language and landscape both changed after the captivity, restricts “his disciples” to the constant companions who lived under one roof, and agrees the sanctification was voluntary, the Evangelist writing many and not all.
Clarke places the town near Bethel and reports that Christ stayed there two months.

Chrysostom looks at the disciples, troubled to see him save himself by merely human means while the nation kept the feast; Theophylact lays the Passion at the door of the Pharisees rather than the people’s ignorance.

Origen reads the retreat as figure — the Word ceasing to walk openly among that people and going to Ephraim, whose name means fruitfulness, when Manasseh, the forgotten elder, was passed over — and notes the Evangelist calls the feast the Jews’ passover and not the Lord’s.

Augustine defends the withdrawal as example, since whoever causes another’s sin is answerable for it, and contrasts a passover kept in the dark with doorposts stained by a slain animal against one kept in the light; Alcuin turns the search around, that they sought him with bad intent while we seek him in God’s temple.

debates.question: Was any purification actually required before the passover?

positions.view: Yes, with graduated times set by the nature of the defilement
No special rite, only the general requirement of cleanness, and this undertaken voluntarily

outliers.claim: Makes the retirement a lesson in not multiplying another man’s guilt: it is praiseworthy to confess when the struggle comes, and no less praiseworthy to avoid giving occasion for it.

themes: Jesus therefore walked no more openly among the Jews; but went thence unto a country near to the wilderness, into a city called Ephraim, and there continued with his disciples.
And the Jews’ passover was nigh at hand: and many went out of the country up to Jerusalem before the passover, to purify themselves.
Then sought they for Jesus, and spake among themselves, as they stood in the temple, What think ye, that he will not come to the feast?
Now both the chief priests and the Pharisees had given a commandment, that, if any man knew where he were, he should shew it, that they might take him.
